title: TB0-10072
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (herein the "claimant") is a citizen of Syria. He claims protection under ss. 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS (from Personal Information Form narrative):

The claimant is Kurdish. His brother was detained and abused, then killed in 1993 fighting for Kurds. His other brother was also detained and abused, and the family got a letter that he joined the peshmerga, the Kurdish resistance, and then disappeared. The mukhabarat, Syrian Intelligence, at times arrested the claimant's father and other brother, looking for the brother who disappeared.

The claimant took Kurdish lessons with an Iraqi Kurd. In the winter of 1995 the house where he learned was raided, and the claimant was detained for three months. He was beaten and doused in cold water while in detention.

Later the claimant took an interest in the peaceful though banned Kurdish Yekiti Party. His father was worried and encouraged him to leave Syria. Thus in January 2005 the claimant went to Greece and made a refugee claim. He was allowed to stay on a series of temporary visas. After two years he wanted to return to Syria, even though he heard the mukhabarat was inquiring after him. The claimant's brother bribed someone to see if he was wanted. The information received was not encouraging, but he snuck into Syria.

After returning to Syria the claimant attended meetings and donated money to the Yekiti cause. On XXXX XXXX, 2008 their house was raided, Kurdish books were found, and the claimant was detained and beaten until XXXX XXXX, 2008.

On XXXX XXXX, 2008 the claimant was arrested, detained and beaten, and released by bribe on XXXX XXXX, 2009. He was released on condition that he report. The mukhabarat came to his house wanting him to sign a document acknowledging a court date.
Thus, the claimant decided to leave Syria. His brother XXXX XXXX to pay a smuggler. The claimant went to Greece but decided not to stay there due to past experience.

The panel finds the claimant to not be a Convention refugee under Section 96 of the IRPA, as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Syria on any of the five Convention grounds. The panel also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection under Section 97 of the IRPA, as, on a balance of probabilities, his removal to Syria would not subject him personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. The panel's reasons are as follows.

Credibility was the determinative issue in this claim. The panel also considered whether the claimant requires Canada's protection merely because he is a Kurd from Syria. The panel has considered all of the evidence and counsel's post-hearing written submission, including documents, received June 21, 2012. Identity

The claimant's personal identity and his identity as a citizen of Syria have been established by a copy of the claimant's Syrian ID Card and Military Book, contained in Exhibit C-2.2 The panel accepts that the claimant is Kurdish, from the fact that he spoke Kurdish at the hearing. General Comment

The panel wishes to note that it acknowledges that if the Syrian Intelligence, or mukhabarat ("Intelligence" herein), is truly targeting the claimant, then it would appear likely that he would be a Convention refugee. It is noted that they can be brutal, use torture, beatings and detentions, all extra-judicially.

The panel took note of the detailed narration of torture the claimant alleged he received. This would be consistent with the documentation before the panel, and had that been the only evidence the panel considered, he would have been found to be a Convention refugee.

However, there were significant problems with the claimant's other evidence, relating to credibility. While the panel would have preferred to be able to accept the claimant's allegations, it simply cannot in the face of the significant credibility issues. The panel is required to gauge credibility. The panel cannot of course ever be absolutely certain that a claimant is not telling the truth. However, if the credibility concerns are serious enough, then the panel can find the claimant to be not credible, and has done so here. The panel is aware of the hypothetical danger to a claimant deemed to be an opponent of the Syrian regime, and thus it would not have made the negative credibility finding unless it were sufficiently confident it was fair and justified.

Conversely, in regard to the brutal nature of Intelligence, this finding works against the claimant as well. There is an issue in regard to re-availment, as will be noted, in that the claimant elected to return to Syria even after being allegedly brutalized by Intelligence, and even not being certain he would not be targeted.

The panel also notes that the claimant testified in a poor manner. On a number of occasions, he had to be asked the same question several times before he answered. It was not suggested that there was any psychological reasons for the claimant's poor testimony. The panel will not make a negative inference as to credibility from the claimant's poor demeanor. However, the panel must note that the claimant's poor demeanor was an impediment to the panel possibly being swayed by the claimant's testimony, even with the quantifiable credibility concerns.

Similarly, the claimant was substantially unable to corroborate his allegations of detention and maltreatment by the regime by independent documentary evidence. It is possible that even if the claimant's allegations were true, they could not be properly documented. As such, the panel will not make any negative inference as to credibility from the claimant's failure to corroborate the alleged detentions and abuse. However, as above, an opportunity was lost for the panel to be convinced that these events did occur, even in the face of other credibility concerns.

The panel finally notes that Syria is currently under revolution. However, the panel finds that this does not impact this refugee claim. Any danger due to fighting, the panel finds, is in the nature of a generalized risk, one shared by all citizens of Syria.

The claimant indicated that he made an asylum claim in Greece in 2005. However, he could not produce any documentation in that regard. This would have been helpful, as the panel would have thus been able to examine the allegations made there, and here, and compare them for consistency. The claimant indicated that there never was a hearing, or a document filled out comparable to the Personal Information Form (PIF), and thus there was nothing to supply in this regard. However, the panel will not make any negative inference as to credibility from this.

The claimant was simply asked his age, and he said he was 32. However, he was 31 at the time of the hearing, and he was asked why he said he was 32. He said all his mind is with his situation and his country. While this point is not relevant to his claim, and the panel will not make any negative inference as to credibility from this, the panel has chosen to mention this to further illustrate how generally unreliable the claimant's testimony, and evidence, appeared to be.

The basis of this claim is that Intelligence is interested in the claimant's family due to their alleged involvement in Kurdish causes. In paragraph 3 of his narrative the claimant alleged that in 1997 the family received a letter from the claimant's brother indicating that the brother joined the peshmarga, or Kurdish resistance movement. The claimant was unable to produce this letter. The panel will not make any negative inference as to credibility from this. However, again, an opportunity was lost for the claimant to buttress his claim in this manner.

The claimant was asked when he was first detained, and he said it was in 1995. He could not document this alleged detention by any document from the authorities or by any medical report, as he said he just applied cream for his injuries. However, there is another issue in regard to this alleged detention. Exhibit R/A-2 contains the form IMM 5611, information the claimant gave to Immigration when he made his refugee claim. In question 37, the claimant was asked if he had ever been arrested, detained or sought by the police, the army or any other authority. The claimant indicated that he had, and enumerated and briefly described the two alleged detentions in 2008. In fact, he referred to the alleged 2008-2009 detention as "the second time."

Thus, the claimant failed to mention the alleged 1995 detention, allegedly having a significant duration of three months. He was asked why he did not mention it. His answers did not explain the omission. He said he just said he was detained twice. He said he was asked to go to court, and then he ran away. This was non-responsive. As he claimed to not understand the question, it was asked again. It was further pointed out to him that in IMM 5611 he was able to supply Immigration with other information, such as his occupation and residence, going back ten years, including his address and the name of his employer in Greece as of 2005, quite a number of years ago. This time the claimant blamed the omission on a lack of sleep. However, in the Minister's Delegate Notes in Exhibit R/A-2, it was not indicated that he asked for time to sleep as he alleged, and the claimant confirmed that it was not on the record.

The panel cannot accept this explanation. The claimant specifically stated that he was detained twice, yet in his PIF alleged that he was detained three times. The omitted detention allegedly lasted three months, and during it the claimant alleged that he was physically abused. The panel finds that if the detention occurred, then the claimant would have remembered it, and would not have failed to mention it, while detailing two subsequent detentions. He claimed to have been sleepy, but was able to describe the other two alleged detentions, and other items going back a number of years. The panel is aware that the alleged detention was in 1995, when the claimant was 14 or so. However, for a youth of such age to be detained and abused in such manner, the panel finds, is not something a person would forget. Thus, from this omission, and/or from the later addition of this allegation in the PIF, the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

The claimant alleged that he went to Greece and made an asylum claim, and he was asked the result of this asylum claim. He said he was not sure. He said he thought his claim was rejected, but it was not refused, and he was not asked to leave Greece. Generally, he said, he was pretty well ignored. He said the claim was still pending when he left Greece, and in fact could still be pending. When asked if he possibly could have been accepted as a refugee in Greece, the claimant said Greece does not accept anyone as refugees. He was thus asked why he went there, and he did not answer directly - he said he tried to go on to Germany, but was unable to, so he stayed in Greece, and made a claim so he would not be arrested.

To summarize the evidence, the claimant fled Syria to Europe, and ended up staying in Greece and making an asylum claim. His father advised him to go to Europe, and the claimant agreed with his father, he said, because the claimant as well feared remaining in Syria. He was probably not accepted in Greece, but he was not asked to leave. It would appear as if the claimant could have stayed in Greece had he wished to. However, he elected to re-avail to Syria, the country from which he had fled, and this re-availment was discussed.

The claimant was asked if he did research on whether it was safe to return to Syria. He indicated that his brother bribed someone to find out if he was wanted, and apparently he was not. Thus, he decided to return to Syria. However, as indicated in his narrative, the claimant still felt it was dangerous, so he decided he had to sneak into Syria rather than report at a Port of Entry. He further indicated in testimony that he had also heard that Intelligence had inquired after him, twice, while he was in Greece. The claimant was asked why, given the above concerns and dangers, he decided to return to Syria. His answers were vague, non-responsive and possibly evasive. Generally, his reply seemed to be that the Intelligence was looking for people in the area generally, but not only him. A significant reason, he said, why he returned, was because he was not treated well in Greece in terms of work and status, and wanted to return home.

The panel, unfortunately, cannot accept these explanations. The claimant had allegedly been detained for some three months prior to his going to and returning from Greece, and mistreated during this detention, the detention he failed to mention in IMM 5611. As indicated above, if this had occurred, the claimant would not have forgotten it. Nor would have the claimant forgotten, the panel finds, how dangerous the Intelligence can be. The claimant was not being asked to leave Greece, and he had an asylum under process. He left Syria due to his father's fear for him, and he said he shared that fear for himself. He said he inquired whether he was wanted in Syria, but he returned there even though Intelligence had been inquiring about him. Even then, he felt he had to sneak into Syria.

All the above demonstrates that the claimant did not have a subjective fear of returning to Syria, and the panel so finds. However, the claimant went back there, abandoning his Greek asylum claim. He claims to have feared Syria, and from this inconsistency the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. The panel notes that at this time the claimant was in his late 20s, a mature adult, and thus this decision cannot be blamed on his youth.

The claimant claimed to have made donations to the Yekiti Party, but could provide no receipts to evidence this. Similarly, as indicated above, he could not document the two alleged detentions in 2008, the ones he remembered when completing IMM 5611. The claimant did indicate, though, that he sought and received medical attention for injuries received during the second detention, in 2008-2009. He said he went to a Kurdish doctor, and he indicated he might be able to provide a medical report in this regard, post-hearing. The claimant and counsel were given time post-hearing to provide such documentation, and in fact a medical note was provided. However, the panel gives this medical note lesser weight than it otherwise would, for the following reason. The claimant was asked why he did not mention in his narrative that he received such medical attention for his injuries, as required in the instructions to s.31 of his PIF. He answered that he just wrote down what happened in jail, which was non-responsive. The panel notes that the claimant was represented by counsel when he prepared his PIF.

At the hearing, the claimant made a very significant amendment to paragraph 15 of his narrative. He changed the date of alleged release from his last alleged detention from XXXX XXXX, 2009 to XXXX XXXX XXXX2009. It is noted that he alleged that his detention started on XXXX XXXX, 2008. The effect of this amendment at the hearing was that the length of the detention was changed from about a month to about two months. This is important because in IMM 5611 the claimant had indicated in regard to this detention: "I was just (sic) spent two months in jail."

The claimant was thus asked why he originally indicated in his narrative that he was released on XXXX XXXX, if the actual date was XXXX XXXX. He blamed this on the translation services when he prepared his narrative in conjunction with counsel's office. He was asked to confirm that Syria uses the same Gregorian calendar as is used in Canada, and he said it is so, except that numbers of months are given instead of months (that is, January would be I, February II, etc.). The panel incidentally notes that any confusion in regard to months would not explain the difference in dates, i.e, 26th from 24th. In any event, it was pointed out to the claimant that when he signed his PIF, he had indicated thereon that it was true and correct, and that he understood it. To this the claimant said that in fact he told the interpreter when he was preparing the PIF that the correct date was February 26, and the interpreter said he would make the correction. The claimant indicated that counsel was there when he told the interpreter this. Counsel indicated at the hearing that if he had been aware of the discrepancy at the time of PIF preparation, as the claimant alleged he was, then he would have changed it in the PIF. This was not done. The claimant was asked, then, why he signed the PIF as it was if the allegedly promised correction had not been made. He said he wrote the narrative in Arabic correctly. However, the claimant did not produce his original Arabic narrative which he presumably wrote himself, in draft, and this could have been helpful, as the Kurdish interpreter at the hearing also was an Arabic speaker.

As such, the panel cannot accept the claimant's explanation, and thus from this very significant inconsistency the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. The panel incidentally notes another problem in regard to the claimant's description of this alleged detention. Counsel asked him when he was detained, and the claimant said it was on XXXX XXXX. When asked to confirm, he quickly changed it to what he originally alleged, XXXX XXXX. While the panel will not make a negative inference as to credibility from this, the panel has mentioned it to further stress the general unreliability of the claimant's testimony.

The claimant alleged that he was released from detention on XXXX XXXX, 2009, as indicated above, and he was asked to indicate what the conditions of his release were. Three times he was asked the question, and did not answer directly at all. Finally, counsel suggested that he did not understand the question, so counsel asked it again. The claimant finally gave part of the answer as indicated in his narrative, but did not mention that he had to inform the regime of his changes of address. When counsel later questioned him on this, the claimant was able to remember that he was required to provide any address changes. The panel will not make a negative inference as to credibility from this, but again points it out to demonstrate the general weakness of the claimant's testimony. The claimant incidentally could not document these alleged terms of release.

Given the above manifold concerns in regard to credibility, the panel finds the claimant's evidence, overall, to be not credible, and thus insufficient to support his claim for refugee protection. DEMONSTRATION(S) IN CANADA, THE CLAIMANT'S IDENTITY AS A KURD

In Exhibit C-2 there are photos of the claimant at an anti-Syrian regime demonstration in Canada. This would raise a potential sur place claim. The claimant said his friend took these photos of him. He was asked if any images of him were broadcast on the internet, such that the regime in Syria might see them. The claimant said that XXXX XXXX, the author of the Kurdish identity letter in Exhibit C-7, posted the images of him on the net, and that he would be able to provide confirmation of same post-hearing. The claimant and counsel were given time post-hearing to provide such documentation, and in fact a DVD of a demonstration was provided, which counsel indicated that the claimant briefly appears in. However, that image would be of the claimant, and counsel did not indicate that the claimant was identified by name. Thus, the panel finds that even if the Syrian regime were hypothetically scouring the internet to see who might be demonstrating against them in Canada, they would not be able to identify the claimant by name, and thus they would not flag him as anti-regime in their computer. In that regard, the panel notes the affidavit by XXXX XXXXin the submission, where this person alleges that his family was detained because XXXX. XXXXallegedly participated in anti-Syrian regimes in Toronto. The panel obviously did not have the opportunity to question XXXX XXXX XXXX, and it appears from his letter that he participated in multiple demonstrations in Toronto, whereas the claimant appeared to have participated in fewer demonstrations. Also, considering the other credibility concerns herein, the panel assigns this letter from XXXX XXXX XXXXlesser weight than it otherwise would have. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Syrian regime would not flag the claimant as anti-regime merely because he participated in a small number of anti-regime demonstrations in Toronto, particularly in light of the fact that it was alleged by the claimant that his personal identity was not revealed.

The claimant indicated that his name was not put on the internet. He said he did not know if the Syrian regime would or could find out about his participation in this rally, but he was afraid they would. The claimant was unable to explain how the Syrian regime could hypothetically identify him from his image, even if it was broadcast. All he could guess was that maybe they would ask people in Canada, who might identify him. The panel does not find it likely that opponents of the regime in Canada would speak to Syrian agents here, if there are any, and inform on one of their colleagues who demonstrated with them against the Syrian regime. The claimant was asked if he has heard of the regime punishing people in Canada, or their families in Syria, for participation in anti-Syrian regimes in Canada, and he said he has. He indicated that he could provide articles in this regard. The claimant and counsel were given time post-hearing to provide such documentation, but it was not provided, nor any explanation in that regard (except for the affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX, discussed above). The claimant indicated at the hearing that he has not heard of any Syrian who was harmed upon a return to Syria for participating in any demonstrations in Canada.

In any event, the panel finds that the Syrian regime would not be able to identify the claimant simply from a photo, if they ever looked at it; thus, the panel finds that the claimant would not be persecuted in Syria for participation in these demonstration(s).

The panel does note that the claimant is Kurdish, and the claimant indicated that is a reason he was arrested and detained. As such, the panel has examined the documentation before it to determine if the claimant requires Canada's protection from Syria simply because he is a Kurd. In that regard, the panel examined Item 2.9 of Exhibit R/A-1, the UK Home Office Operational Guidance Note. It indicates that Kurds constitute about 8-15% of the population of Syria, or about 1.75 million people. The report indicates that there is some discrimination against Kurds; however, persecution arises when the regime had identified a person as being a member of an anti-regime organization. The credibility analysis above has led to a finding that the claimant has not been so identified by the regime. Item 2.4 of Exhibit R/A-1, the UK Home Office Country of Origin Report, confirms this, and further indicates that the regime will persecute people if they are suspected to be separatists. This results in an intolerance of Kurdish cultural activities, which are suspected of being nationalist or separatist in nature. However, again, the panel has rejected the argument that the claimant is wanted for anti-regime activities or affiliation.

The panel has also reviewed Exhibit C-4, some articles submitted by counsel in regard to the situation of Kurds. These articles echo what is referred to above. They confirm the regime will persecute Kurdish activists and party members. They further confirm that the regime restricts cultural expression by Kurds. However, as above, the panel finds the latter to be discrimination, and notes again that it has rejected the allegations that the claimant would be targeted because of his affiliation with his family, which allegedly included Kurd activists and fighters.
Thus, the panel finds that the claimant does not require Canada's protection merely because he is of Kurdish ethnicity.

For the foregoing reasons, the panel finds the claimant to not be a Convention refugee under s. 96, nor a person in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA. For these reasons, the claim is rejected. (signed) "M. Sterlin" M.
